1929-1937

Caption This

The Great Depression and the New Deal

15

How this works (15–20 minutes)

  1. Look at each of the 5 images. Read the “What you’re looking at” line.
  2. Write a short, funny caption, like a meme. Pick a caption style if you want one.
  3. Then write 2–3 sentences about what is really going on. Use at least one key term from the lesson. Type the key term in English, exactly as shown.
  4. Save Progress any time. When all 5 are done, press Finished and upload the file to Canvas.

Keep it respectful: make the joke about the company, the idea, or the situation. Never joke about workers, children, immigrants, enslaved or freed people, Native peoples, anyone’s race or religion, or people who were hurt.

Image 1 of 5

Black Tuesday on Wall Street

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 23. A huge crowd of men in hats and coats fills a street beside a big stone building. Old cars and a horse stand at the left. A sign in the crowd says “Caution: Speed limit 8 miles per hour. Axle load restricted to 10 tons.” Norton says this is a panicked crowd of shareholders and investors outside the Stock Exchange on Wall Street in New York on October 29, 1929.

Heads up: Many people in this crowd were losing their savings. Aim your joke at the stock market, the sign, or the sea of hats. Never joke about people who lost their money or their jobs.

  • Look at the sign on the right. What does it say? Why is it odd to see that sign next to this crowd?
  • Look at the crowd. What do you think these people are waiting to hear?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Great Depression (1929–1941)Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) (1934)
Image 2 of 5

“Okies on the Run”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 23. An old open car is packed with people and belongings. Adults and children sit inside, and some of the children are eating. A box of Scotch Soap, a metal pot, bags, and a metal case are tied onto the car with rope. A man in a sun hat stands at the left. Norton says this sharecropping family has reached Bakersfield, California, in 1935 after they “got blowed out in Oklahoma.”

Heads up: This is a serious one. It shows a real family in real hardship. Write one clear line. No jokes about the family, the children, or anyone who lost a home. Look at the car, the ropes, and the bundles.

  • Look at how the car is loaded. What did the family decide to bring? What did they have to leave behind?
  • Look at the people in the car. What does the photo tell you about their trip?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Dust BowlGreat Depression (1929–1941)
Image 3 of 5

“The Galloping Snail”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white cartoon from Norton Ch. 23. A man with “FDR” on his back rides a giant snail. He holds a whip in one hand and reins in the other. The snail’s shell says “Congressional Action.” The snail has racehorse legs, and dust clouds fly up behind it. A rolled paper that says “New Deal Program” sticks out of the man’s coat. A small domed building is at the lower right. Norton says it is from the Detroit News, March 1933.

Heads up: This cartoon is about a real president, Franklin Roosevelt. Aim your joke at the snail, the whip, the dust, or how fast Congress moves. Never joke about how he looks or about his health or body.

  • Read the words on the snail’s shell. What is the cartoonist saying about Congress?
  • Look at the whip, the dust, and the racehorse legs. Is the snail going fast or slow? What is the cartoonist’s point?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: First New Deal (1933–1935)Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation (FDIC) (1933)
Image 4 of 5

Norris Dam

Not done

What you’re looking at: A black-and-white photograph from Norton Ch. 23. A huge dam wall rises above a construction site. Wooden frames and scaffolds cover the lower part, and ladders run up the slanted face. Tiny workers stand on the frames and the ground below, and boards and rubble are piled in front. Norton says this is Norris Dam in Tennessee, completed in 1936 under the Tennessee Valley Authority.

Heads up: Real workers built this dam, and these jobs mattered to families in the Depression. Aim your joke at the giant wall, the wooden scaffolds, the ladders, or the pile of boards. Never joke about the workers.

  • Find the tiny workers. How big is the dam compared with them?
  • Look at the wooden frames and ladders. What does this tell you about how the dam was built?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: First New Deal (1933–1935)Great Depression (1929–1941)
Image 5 of 5

“A monthly check to you”

Not done

What you’re looking at: A color poster from Norton Ch. 23. Big red letters across the top say “A monthly check to you –”. A hand reaches in from the right and holds a check marked “Your monthly Social Security check.” A building that looks like the U.S. Capitol stands behind it. Words on the left say “For the rest of your life, beginning when you are 65.” A red box at the bottom says who can sign up and how. Norton says the government gave out posters like this to teach people about the new Social Security Act.

Heads up: Social Security was meant to help older Americans. Aim your joke at the giant hand, the check, the Capitol, or the slogan. Never joke about older people or about workers who were left out.

  • Read the big red words and the words on the left. What does the poster promise, and starting when?
  • Find the words “few exceptions” in the red box. Who might be left out?
Pick a caption style (optional)

Key terms that fit this image: Social Security Act (1935)Second New Deal (1935–1938)
